ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Both studies received institutional ethical approval (ref: 15576).
In both studies, participants were recruited to take part in an online RCT where they were required to make hypothetical food choices under different FOPL conditions.
In Study 1 (between-subjects), participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1) using the Qualtrics randomiser function to (1) WL group, (2) TLL group, or (3) no label group (control).

In Study 2 (mixed design) participants completed a baseline food choice task in part one (no label present), before being randomly assigned (1:1:1) using the Qualtrics randomiser function to (1) WL group, (2) TLL group, or (3) no label group (in which they completed the same task a second time).
For both studies, participants were recruited using the online participant panel provider Prolific.
For Study 2, Prolific recruitment was supplemented with targeted social media recruitment (posting in ED support groups on Facebook with permission) and the NIHR Be Part of Research registry.

Be Part of Research is a free UK-wide service from the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), in collaboration with the NHS and the UK's devolved administrationswith over 700,000 volunteers signed up.
Prolific participants were paid at a rate of £6/hr.
Participants recruited outside of Prolific were entered into a prize draw for a £100 Amazon voucher, and £1 was donated to the ED charity 'Beat' for each completed response.
Participants were required to confirm that they had read the information sheet, and consent to taking part, to proceed with the survey.
Participants were shown all six options at once and were asked to choose one item, imagining that they would actually pay for, receive, and eat this item.
Participants were asked to report characteristics including age, sex, ethnicity, race, highest education level and household income.

Participants were asked 'Did you notice a nutrition label when making your food choices (e.g., when choosing crisps, pasta ready meal, cereal, savoury snacks, and lunch salad?' ('yes' / 'no' / 'unsure').
Participants were asked 'Did the presence of a nutrition label on the food items influence your food choice?' ('Yes' / 'No' / 'Unsure').
Participants were asked 'What do you think the aim of this study is?' with an open-text response option.
Participants were also excluded from Study 2 if they did not have usable follow-up data.
A total of 968 participants completed Study 1.
Participants were excluded if they failed both attention checks (n = 25) or reported an ED diagnosis (n = 19).
A total of 403 participants completed Study 2.
Participants were excluded for failing both attention checks (n = 8), not having a confirmed ED diagnosis (n = 66), or not having usable follow-up data (n = 79).
Most of the final sample were recruited through Prolific (n = 168, 70%) followed by social media (n = 58) 24.2%) and the Be Part of Research registry (n = 14, 5.8%).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: For Study 2, to detect a mixed interaction effect of f = 0.12 (or d = 0.24) in our planned ANOVA (p < 0.05, 80% power, GPOWER 3.1), a total sample size of N = 246 is required. We aimed to recruit a minimum of 246 participants and up to a maximum of 400 participants (if feasible during the 3-month data collection period) due to uncertainty around effect size estimation for power calculation (as WL vs. TLL has not previously been tested in an ED population), and possible data exclusions.

For Study 1, to detect a difference of d = 0.24 between conditions in follow-up independent samples t-tests (p < 0.05, 80% power, GPOWER 3.1) requires 274 participants per condition (total N = 822). We therefore aimed to recruit a total of 946 participants to account for loss of data (up to 15%).

For both studies, we powered to our primary outcome (unhealthy food item selection). A metaanalysis found small effects of WL for reducing probability of selecting an unhealthy item relative to a control (OR = 0.65, or d = 0.24) and TLL (OR = 0.81, or d = 0.45) (4).

live_data_statements: In both studies, participants were recruited to take part in an online RCT where they were required to make hypothetical food choices under different FOPL conditions.
In Study 1 (between-subjects), participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1) using the Qualtrics randomiser function to (1) WL group, (2) TLL group, or (3) no label group (control).

In Study 2 (mixed design) participants completed a baseline food choice task in part one (no label present), before being randomly assigned (1:1:1) using the Qualtrics randomiser function to (1) WL group, (2) TLL group, or (3) no label group (in which they completed the same task a second time).
For both studies, participants were recruited using the online participant panel provider Prolific.
For Study 2, Prolific recruitment was supplemented with targeted social media recruitment (posting in ED support groups on Facebook with permission) and the NIHR Be Part of Research registry.

Be Part of Research is a free UK-wide service from the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), in collaboration with the NHS and the UK's devolved administrationswith over 700,000 volunteers signed up.
Prolific participants were paid at a rate of £6/hr.
Participants recruited outside of Prolific were entered into a prize draw for a £100 Amazon voucher, and £1 was donated to the ED charity 'Beat' for each completed response.
Participants were required to confirm that they had read the information sheet, and consent to taking part, to proceed with the survey.
Participants were shown all six options at once and were asked to choose one item, imagining that they would actually pay for, receive, and eat this item.
Participants were asked to report characteristics including age, sex, ethnicity, race, highest education level and household income.

Participants were asked 'Did you notice a nutrition label when making your food choices (e.g., when choosing crisps, pasta ready meal, cereal, savoury snacks, and lunch salad?' ('yes' / 'no' / 'unsure').
Participants were asked 'Did the presence of a nutrition label on the food items influence your food choice?' ('Yes' / 'No' / 'Unsure').
Participants were asked 'What do you think the aim of this study is?' with an open-text response option.
Participants were also excluded from Study 2 if they did not have usable follow-up data.
A total of 968 participants completed Study 1.
Participants were excluded if they failed both attention checks (n = 25) or reported an ED diagnosis (n = 19).
A total of 403 participants completed Study 2.
Participants were excluded for failing both attention checks (n = 8), not having a confirmed ED diagnosis (n = 66), or not having usable follow-up data (n = 79).
Most of the final sample were recruited through Prolific (n = 168, 70%) followed by social media (n = 58) 24.2%) and the Be Part of Research registry (n = 14, 5.8%).

text.text: In the UK, front-of-pack traffic light labels (TLL) are implemented voluntarily.
The UK Government are considering alternative FOP approaches, such as nutrient warning labels (WL).
However, the effects and potential harm of TLL versus WL in UK consumers are unclear.
We compared the effects of WL, TLL, and no label on unhealthy food item selection and negative affect among UK adults with and without an eating disorder (ED).
We conducted two online randomised controlled trials.
In Study 1, 924 UK adults without an ED diagnosis were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to a WL, TLL, or no labels condition and completed a food-choice task.

In Study 2, 240 UK adults with an ED diagnosis completed a baseline no-label food choice task and were subsequently randomly assigned (1:1:1) to WL, TLL, or no labels for a follow-up food choice task.
The primary outcome was the number of task-specific unhealthy food items selected.
Negative affect before and after food choice tasks was measured as a secondary outcome.
In Study 1 (data collected 02/25 -04/25), unhealthy food selection differed by condition (p = .013).
Of five products selected, WL participants selected 0.20 fewer unhealthy items than TLL participants (8.0%; p = .038) and 0.28 fewer than controls (10.7%; p = .004).
In Study 2 (data collected 11/25 -02/26), unhealthy selection decreased by 0.39 items with WL (17.7%; p = .015), 0.13 with TLL (5.3%, p = .286), and 0.00 with no labels.
The reduction was greater with WL than with no labels (p = .029).
Label condition did not differentially affect task-related negative affect in either study (Study 1, p = .757; Study 2, p = .448).
Interpretation WL tended to be associated with lower unhealthy food selection compared to TLL in UK adults.
There was minimal evidence that WL or TLL caused negative emotional responses.
NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.
Rising rates of obesity and non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are a significant public health concern.
Approximately 63% of adults are living with obesity or classified as overweight and 1 in 5 children in England are leaving primary school with obesity (1).
text.formatted: Approximately 63% of adults are living with obesity or classified as overweight and 1 in 5 children in England are leaving primary school with obesity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: The likelihood of obesity is notably higher in areas of greater socioeconomic deprivation, where factors such as limited access to affordable healthy food and safe spaces for physical activity present a challenge (1).
text.formatted: The likelihood of obesity is notably higher in areas of greater socioeconomic deprivation, where factors such as limited access to affordable healthy food and safe spaces for physical activity present a challenge <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Front of pack (FOP) labelling is a public health policy aimed at improving the diet of the UK population by providing comprehensible nutritional information on packaged food products (2).
text.formatted: Front of pack (FOP) labelling is a public health policy aimed at improving the diet of the UK population by providing comprehensible nutritional information on packaged food products <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref>.

text.text: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses conclude that FOP labelling supports consumers to make healthier food choices (3, 4).
text.formatted: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses conclude that FOP labelling supports consumers to make healthier food choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4)</ref>.

text.text: There is also evidence suggesting FOP labelling encourages reformulation of food products, but this varies by FOP label and implementation type (5).
text.formatted: There is also evidence suggesting FOP labelling encourages reformulation of food products, but this varies by FOP label and implementation type <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: In the UK, traffic light labels (TLL) have been implemented as a standardised voluntary FOP labelling system since 2013.
TLL presents nutritional information per portion and uses green, amber, and red colour-coding to indicate if a food item is low, medium, or high in saturated fat, fat, salt, and/or sugar (6).
text.formatted: TLL presents nutritional information per portion and uses green, amber, and red colour-coding to indicate if a food item is low, medium, or high in saturated fat, fat, salt, and/or sugar <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref>.

text.text: Calorie content is also displayed but not colour-coded.
Quasiexperimental evidence suggests that its introduction has improved the nutritional quality of household food purchases (7).
text.formatted: Quasiexperimental evidence suggests that its introduction has improved the nutritional quality of household food purchases <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Chile introduced mandatory FOP nutrient warning labels (WL) on packaged foods high in calories, saturated fat, salt, and/or sugar in 2016 alongside other related policy interventions (8).
text.formatted: Chile introduced mandatory FOP nutrient warning labels (WL) on packaged foods high in calories, saturated fat, salt, and/or sugar in 2016 alongside other related policy interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: Since then, several other counties have adopted or are considering adopting a FOP WL policy, including the UK, to help reduce rates of obesity and related NCDs (2, 9).
text.formatted: Since then, several other counties have adopted or are considering adopting a FOP WL policy, including the UK, to help reduce rates of obesity and related NCDs <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9)</ref>.

text.text: Research postimplementation of mandatory FOP WL has demonstrated a reduction in consumer purchase of high calorie, HFSS foods in addition to reformulation (10) (11) (12).
text.formatted: Research postimplementation of mandatory FOP WL has demonstrated a reduction in consumer purchase of high calorie, HFSS foods in addition to reformulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: There is less research directly comparing effectiveness of TLL and WL.
A systematic review and meta-analysis indicated that while both TLL and WL reduce the probability of selecting an unhealthy item relative to a control, WL perform better than TLL (4).
text.formatted: A systematic review and meta-analysis indicated that while both TLL and WL reduce the probability of selecting an unhealthy item relative to a control, WL perform better than TLL <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: It is theorised that this is due to WL being easier to process and emotionally respond to (e.g., concern about the high nutrient content).

Whereas TLL may be more likely to confuse the participants if a product has, for example, both an amber and green label, which can lead participants to incorrectly perceive a product to be healthier than it is (13).
text.formatted: Whereas TLL may be more likely to confuse the participants if a product has, for example, both an amber and green label, which can lead participants to incorrectly perceive a product to be healthier than it is <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>.

text.text: The detailed numerical information and reference intake percentages displayed on TLL have also been highlighted as a point of confusion (14).
text.formatted: The detailed numerical information and reference intake percentages displayed on TLL have also been highlighted as a point of confusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: However, this comparison was limited to eight studies with heterogenous label formats, position, study population, study design, and experimental settings (4).
There are very few studies comparing TLL and WL directly in a representative UK sample using a realistic food choice task.
Understanding the relative costs and benefits of different FOP labelling systems is important to ensure optimal policy design and implementation.
If labelling systems are well-understood and accepted, then they are more likely to be effective (15).
text.formatted: If labelling systems are well-understood and accepted, then they are more likely to be effective <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, if individuals cannot understand the labelling system or feel annoyed by it, then this could lead to individuals ignoring labelling systems (16).
text.formatted: Conversely, if individuals cannot understand the labelling system or feel annoyed by it, then this could lead to individuals ignoring labelling systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: It is also important to consider how vulnerable groups may respond to different FOP labelling systems.
It is estimated that approximately 3.4 million or 1 in 20 people aged 16 or over in the UK have an eating disorder (ED) (17).
text.formatted: It is estimated that approximately 3.4 million or 1 in 20 people aged 16 or over in the UK have an eating disorder (ED) <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref>.

text.text: People living with an ED are likely to be at increased risk of harm from food labelling.
Most research to date into food labelling and individuals with an ED has centred on response to out-of-home (OOH) calorie labelling (18).
text.formatted: Most research to date into food labelling and individuals with an ED has centred on response to out-of-home (OOH) calorie labelling <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: A systematic review and meta-analysis found that ED pathology was related to being more aware of OOH labels, paying more attention to caloric intake, and adjusting behaviour in response to the labels (18).
text.formatted: A systematic review and meta-analysis found that ED pathology was related to being more aware of OOH labels, paying more attention to caloric intake, and adjusting behaviour in response to the labels <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative findings suggest a polarised response to OOH calorie labels among individuals with an ED, ranging from them being reassuring and giving "a sense of control" to causing emotional distress and negatively impacting ED recovery (19).
text.formatted: Qualitative findings suggest a polarised response to OOH calorie labels among individuals with an ED, ranging from them being reassuring and giving "a sense of control" to causing emotional distress and negatively impacting ED recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: However, limited research has examined how different FOP labelling systems, including WL, may affect the behaviour of people living with an ED (20).
text.formatted: However, limited research has examined how different FOP labelling systems, including WL, may affect the behaviour of people living with an ED <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20)</ref>.

text.text: In a UK context, there is scarce research comparing FOP TLL to WL and no research has examined this in context of people living with an ED.

Therefore, there is a need to (i) understand and compare how these different types of labelling systems influence food choice and (ii) identify any potential unintended psychological consequences, particularly among individuals with an ED.

The present research comprises two online RCTs in which participants made a series of hypothetical supermarket food choices across different food categories that either displayed WL, TLL, or no label (control).
The aims of this work were to compare the impact of TLL and WL on food choice and negative emotional responses in (i) individuals without an ED (Study 1) and (ii) individuals with an ED (Study 2).

Specifically, we hypothesised that both WL and TLL will affect how many unhealthy food items are selected (vs. control), but WL will have a larger impact on discouraging unhealthy food choices than TLL, and WL will have a larger impact on negative emotional responses than TLL.
We also examined calories and nutrients selected, and measures of participant perceived effectiveness and preference for the different FOP labelling systems.
The studies were pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/879kh) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07339969).
text.formatted: The studies were pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/879kh">https://osf.io/879kh</ref>) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07339969).

text.text: Both studies received institutional ethical approval (ref: 15576).
In both studies, participants were recruited to take part in an online RCT where they were required to make hypothetical food choices under different FOPL conditions.
In Study 1 (between-subjects), participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1) using the Qualtrics randomiser function to (1) WL group, (2) TLL group, or (3) no label group (control).

In Study 2 (mixed design) participants completed a baseline food choice task in part one (no label present), before being randomly assigned (1:1:1) using the Qualtrics randomiser function to (1) WL group, (2) TLL group, or (3) no label group (in which they completed the same task a second time).
The second part was required to be completed between 24 hours and 1 week after completing the baseline task.
A mixed design was adopted for Study 2 to increase statistical power, because it was not feasible to recruit a similarly large sample as Study 1 when restricted only to participants with an ED.
For Study 1, the inclusion criteria were current UK resident; over 18 years of age; fluent in English.

The exclusion criteria were fasting or other form of restrictive eating e.g., intermittent fasting, elimination diet (FODMAP), religious restrictions, allergy restrictions, calorie/macronutrient restriction, food group restriction; clinical ED or disordered eating; dietary restrictions/intolerances including Vegan, Vegetarian, Gluten-free, Dairy-Free, Sugar-Free, Low salt.
Recruitment was also stratified to be representative of the UK population in terms of sex, age, and education level (21) (22) (23), see Appendix A for specific stratification plan.
text.formatted: Recruitment was also stratified to be representative of the UK population in terms of sex, age, and education level <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23)</ref>, see Appendix A for specific stratification plan.

text.text: For Study 2, the inclusion and exclusion criteria were the same as for Study 1, except a current or past ED diagnosis was part of the inclusion criteria.
For both studies, participants were recruited using the online participant panel provider Prolific.
For Study 2, Prolific recruitment was supplemented with targeted social media recruitment (posting in ED support groups on Facebook with permission) and the NIHR Be Part of Research registry.

Be Part of Research is a free UK-wide service from the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), in collaboration with the NHS and the UK's devolved administrationswith over 700,000 volunteers signed up.

Individuals that were registered with Be Part of Research who expressed an interest in taking part in research relating to 'eating disorders' were identified by the service and sent information about the opportunity to take part in the study.
Prolific participants were paid at a rate of £6/hr.
Participants recruited outside of Prolific were entered into a prize draw for a £100 Amazon voucher, and £1 was donated to the ED charity 'Beat' for each completed response.
Procedures Qualtrics XM survey software was used to create the survey questions and different trials within the food choice task.
An online information sheet and consent form were automatically displayed to participants via Qualtrics before the survey started.
Participants were required to confirm that they had read the information sheet, and consent to taking part, to proceed with the survey.
The survey took approximately 15 minutes to complete.
Upon completion of the survey, an online debrief sheet was displayed.

In Study 2, an exit button was present on all pages which automatically directed participants to the debrief form, which included links to relevant support pages/phone numbers if the survey had triggered ED symptoms.
Each participant, irrespective of the group completed five trials within the main task.

Participants viewed a selection of six packaged food items for scenarios involving labels predominately relating to (1) sugar (cereal), (2) salt (crisps), (3) fat (assorted savoury snacks), (4) saturated fat (pasta ready meals), and (5) calorie content (lunch salads) of the food products.
Products were kept as similar as possible within each trial.
For example, all cereals were chocolate flavoured and all crisps were salt and vinegar flavoured.

Across the five scenarios, eleven products (36.7%) were not high in any nutrient, eleven (36.7%) were high in one nutrient, six (20.0%) were high in two nutrients, and two (6.7%) were high in three nutrients.
See Appendix B for included items and 'high in' nutrient distribution per task.
Pricing was not displayed to isolate the impact of the labels on food choice.
For each scenario, three items were 'high in' the key nutrient (e.g., sugar for the cereal scenario) and three items were not high in that nutrient.
Criteria for products labelled 'high in' was consistent with labelling criteria for a red TLL in the UK; >25% of the nutrient reference intake per 100g, or >30% per portion (24).
text.formatted: Criteria for products labelled 'high in' was consistent with labelling criteria for a red TLL in the UK; >25% of the nutrient reference intake per 100g, or >30% per portion <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref>.

text.text: For the calorie content scenario only, >25% per 100g / portion (after rounding) was considered 'high in'.
text.formatted: For the calorie content scenario only, >25% per 100g / portion (after rounding) was considered 'high in'.

text.text: The design of the WL was informed by the results from patient and public involvement (PPI) from a study co-designing and testing 'high in' WLs for food items in the UK (25).
text.formatted: The design of the WL was informed by the results from patient and public involvement (PPI) from a study co-designing and testing 'high in' WLs for food items in the UK <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>.

text.text: The design of TLL was as it exists on UK products currently, except calorie information was removed for all scenarios apart from the calorie-specific (lunch salads) scenario, in which calorie information was also colour-coded.
Packaged products were selected from Tesco online supermarket.
Label height was matched across TLL and WL conditions and was approximately consistent with TLL label size and placement on the Tesco website.
Participants were shown all six options at once and were asked to choose one item, imagining that they would actually pay for, receive, and eat this item.
In total, participants chose five different items, one from each trial.
After participants made their food choices, they were asked questions about the task they had just completed.
The tasks and questionnaires were identical in Study 1 and Study 2, unless indicated.
Participants were asked to report characteristics including age, sex, ethnicity, race, highest education level and household income.
Education and household income were measured to characterise SEP.
Self-reported weight and height were asked to calculate body mass index (BMI).
Participants in Study 2 also reported the specific ED they have been diagnosed with.
The Food Choice Questionnaire (FCQ) assesses the motives influencing an individual's food choices (26).
text.formatted: The Food Choice Questionnaire (FCQ) assesses the motives influencing an individual's food choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26)</ref>.

text.text: We included the health motives scale as health motivated individuals may be more likely to pay attention to and be influenced by a nutrition label when making food choices.
The five items that measure health motives were included; mean score was calculated with a higher score indicating greater health motives.
The EDE-QS is a shorter version of the EDE-Q which provides a single overall score reflecting general ED symptom severity (27).
text.formatted: The EDE-QS is a shorter version of the EDE-Q which provides a single overall score reflecting general ED symptom severity <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27)</ref>.

text.text: This 12-item questionnaire with responses rated on a 4-point Likert scale, ranging from 0 ('not at all' / '0 days') to 3 ('markedly' / '6-7 days') was administered.
The mean response to the 12 items was calculated.
Higher scores indicate higher ED symptomatology.
Total number of unhealthy food items selected Total number of selected unhealthy food items across the 5 trials (0-5).
Unhealthy food items were coded as items eligible for a WL or a red TLL for the task-specific nutrient e.g., red for salt in the crisps trial.
Total calories and nutrients from selected food items Total number of calories, salt (g), sugar (g), fat (g), saturated fat (g) from selected food items across the 5 trials was calculated.
Positive and negative affect schedule (PANAS) Negative affect was assessed using the five PANAS items corresponding to negative affect (29).
text.formatted: Positive and negative affect schedule (PANAS) Negative affect was assessed using the five PANAS items corresponding to negative affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref>.

text.text: These items were included pre-and post-food choice task.
Responses to 'How afraid/upset/nervous/scared/distressed do you feel right now?' were conveyed using a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 ('Very slightly or not at all') to 5 ('Extremely').
Mean pre-and postfood choice task scores were calculated, with a higher score indicating greater negative affect.
Negative arousal An adapted four-item measure, previously used to assess responses to health WLs regarding snack selection (28) was included.
text.formatted: Negative arousal An adapted four-item measure, previously used to assess responses to health WLs regarding snack selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref> was included.

text.text: Responses were conveyed using seven-point scales: 'How afraid/worried/uncomfortable/disgusted does the label on food make you feel about consuming the product?
With scores ranging from 1 (not at all afraid/worried/uncomfortable/disgusted) to 7 (very afraid/worried/uncomfortable/disgusted).
A mean score was calculated for the four items, with a higher score indicating greater negative arousal.

text.text: Responses were examined using a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 ('not annoying' / 'not at all') to 7 ('extremely annoying' / 'very likely').
Items were scored separately with a higher score indicating greater reactance / avoidance.
Acceptability was assessed using the item 'Do you support or oppose putting this label on food products?' .
Responses were examined on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 ('strongly oppose') to 7 ('strongly support').
A higher score indicates greater support for the label.
The three-item UNC PME scale was adapted for use (25, 30).

text.text: The three items were Discouragement: 'This label discourages me from wanting to consume a food product'.
Unpleasantness: 'The label makes consuming a food product seem unpleasant'.
Concern: 'This label makes me concerned about the health effects of consuming a food product'.
Responses were conveyed using a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1('not at all') to 5 ('a great deal').
The mean response across the three items was calculated, with a higher score indicating higher PME.

Participants were asked 'Did you notice a nutrition label when making your food choices (e.g., when choosing crisps, pasta ready meal, cereal, savoury snacks, and lunch salad?' ('yes' / 'no' / 'unsure').
Participants were asked 'Did the presence of a nutrition label on the food items influence your food choice?' ('Yes' / 'No' / 'Unsure').
If 'yes', how did the nutrition label influence your food choice?

Response options (order of presentation randomised): 'it made me select a healthier food item' / 'it made me avoid items high in fat/saturated fat/salt/sugar' / 'it made me select a less healthy food item' / 'it prompted me to think about my food choice before deciding' / 'it didn't influence me and I ignored it' / 'not sure'.
Participants were asked 'What do you think the aim of this study is?' with an open-text response option.
Two researchers independently coded study aim awareness ('aware' / 'unaware') and resolved any disagreements through discussion.
To be coded as 'aware', responses were required to mention the impact of labelling on food choice / emotion (or similar).
Descriptive statistics were used to summarise participant characteristics, as well as primary, secondary, and additional outcomes.
Continuous variables are summarised as means and standard deviations, and categorical variables are summarised as counts and percentages, split by labelling condition and overall.
Results from primary analysis were considered significant at p <.05.

text.text: A one-way ANOVA was used to assess the difference between the number of unhealthy food items selected in the three label conditions.

Separate one-way ANOVAs were used to assess the impact of the different label conditions on (i) total fat, saturated fat, sugar, salt, and calories in selected items, (ii) negative arousal (iii) reactance, (iv) avoidance, (v) acceptability and (vi) perceived message effectiveness.
A mixed ANOVA (within-subject factor: time point of negative affect rating, between-subjects factor: condition) was used to assess the impact of different label conditions on negative affect.

Separate ANOVAs were used to assess interaction effects between label condition and relevant participant characteristics (age, sex, highest education, household income, health motives) in terms of (i) number of labelled items selected and (ii) negative affect.

For all primary, secondary, and exploratory analyses, planned follow-up t-test comparisons were used for any significant main effects or interactions (where relevant) to examine specific differences between the three label conditions.

Sensitivity analyses were conducted with aim guessers removed for primary and secondary analyses, to assess if results were the same after removing any participants that correctly guessed the study aims.

Analyses were the same as for Study 1, except mixed ANOVAs were used for outcomes measured at both baseline and follow-up, with time point as the within-subjects factor and label condition as the between-subjects factor.
The condition x time interaction assessed whether change from baseline to follow-up differed between the three label conditions.

For change in negative affect, a 3 x 2 x 2 mixed ANOVA was conducted, with condition as the between-subjects factor and time (pre-task or post-task) and session (baseline or follow-up) as within-subjects factors.
For exploratory moderation analyses, interactions between condition, time and the relevant participant characteristic were examined.
Outcomes assessed only at follow-up (e.g., negative arousal in response to the label) were analysed using between-subject ANOVAs.
Baseline-adjusted ANCOVAs were conducted as sensitivity analyses for outcomes measured at both baseline and follow-up (see Appendix E).

Participant data was excluded from relevant analyses if they (i) did not meet the inclusion criteria, (ii) failed both attention checks, and/or (iii) provided a data point deemed to be an outlier (> 2.5 the median absolute deviation [MAD] value from condition median) for primary or secondary outcomes (31).

text.text: Participants were also excluded from Study 2 if they did not have usable follow-up data.
For both studies, we powered to our primary outcome (unhealthy food item selection).
A metaanalysis found small effects of WL for reducing probability of selecting an unhealthy item relative to a control (OR = 0.65, or d = 0.24) and TLL (OR = 0.81, or d = 0.45) (4).
For Study 1, to detect a difference of d = 0.24 between conditions in follow-up independent samples t-tests (p < 0.05, 80% power, GPOWER 3.1) requires 274 participants per condition (total N = 822).

text.text: We therefore aimed to recruit a total of 946 participants to account for loss of data (up to 15%).
For Study 2, to detect a mixed interaction effect of f = 0.12 (or d = 0.24) in our planned ANOVA (p < 0.05, 80% power, GPOWER 3.1), a total sample size of N = 246 is required.

TLL has not previously been tested in an ED population), and possible data exclusions.
A total of 968 participants completed Study 1.
Participants were excluded if they failed both attention checks (n = 25) or reported an ED diagnosis (n = 19).
This resulted in a final analytic sample of 924 participants.
A total of 403 participants completed Study 2.
Participants were excluded for failing both attention checks (n = 8), not having a confirmed ED diagnosis (n = 66), or not having usable follow-up data (n = 79).
This resulted in a final analytic sample of 240 participants.
Most of the final sample were recruited through Prolific (n = 168, 70%) followed by social media (n = 58) 24.2%) and the Be Part of Research registry (n = 14, 5.8%).

Exploratory analyses examined whether age, sex, highest education (bachelor's degree or above versus no bachelor's degree), household income category score, and health-related food choice motives moderated the effect of label condition on unhealthy food-item selection and change in negative affect.

text.text: Across Study 1 and 2, WL tended to outperform TLL in terms of reducing unhealthy item selection, and the amount of saturated fat and salt selected (Study 2 only).

Conversely, TLL was perceived by participants to be more effective than WL for discouraging unhealthy food selection in the sample without an ED diagnosis and also preferred as a labelling format in both samples.
In both studies we found no evidence that negative affect increased as a result of exposure to either labelling type.

Together, findings suggest that among studied UK adults WL is most effective for changing food choice and TLL was generally preferred by participants, but neither appear to cause unintended psychological harm.
These findings are consistent with a small number of studies which indicate WL may outperform TLL in terms of reducing unhealthy food choice (3, 4).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with a small number of studies which indicate WL may outperform TLL in terms of reducing unhealthy food choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4)</ref>.

text.text: We replicate these findings in a UK sample specifically, and tentatively in a UK sample with an ED diagnosis.
Participants in both samples indicated greater support for TLL relative to WL as a FOP labelling policy, and this was particularly evident among participants with an ED.
Participants without an ED perceived TLL to be more effective than WL, although there was no difference for participants with an ED.
Theoretically it would make sense for WL to be perceived as more effective due to clearer indication of the (un)healthfulness of the product (4).
It may be that because the TLL has been implemented voluntarily in the UK since 2013, UK consumers are more familiar with this label and therefore view it more favourably.
In terms of negative emotional responses to the labels, neither TLL nor WL appeared to evoke negative arousal relative to no label.
When compared to each other, negative arousal was higher for TLL than WL among participants without an ED, but not among participants with an ED.
Psychological reactance was higher for WL than TLL for participants with an ED, but there was no difference for participants without an ED.
Other comparisons (e.g., avoidance) revealed no differences between labels or study populations.
While the above outcomes produced inconsistent evidence, no change in negative affect was observed before and after being exposed to either of the labels.
Collectively these findings suggest that neither acute exposure to TLL nor WL elicits notable increases in negative affect, including among individuals with an ED.
This is contrary to related qualitative research which indicates that OOH calorie labelling causes emotional distress among individuals with an ED (19).
text.formatted: This is contrary to related qualitative research which indicates that OOH calorie labelling causes emotional distress among individuals with an ED <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: It may be that because TLL and WL do not specifically focus on calories they are less distressing.
The majority female and younger age distribution of participants in Study 2 is representative of the demographics of people with an ED in the UK (17).
text.formatted: The majority female and younger age distribution of participants in Study 2 is representative of the demographics of people with an ED in the UK <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref>.

text.text: However, this sample were also predominantly degree educated.
There is limited data available on ED prevalence and education, but ED is known to impact individuals across all educational backgrounds, so this may limit generalisability.
The ED sample consisted predominantly of participants reporting diagnoses of anorexia, binge eating disorder and/or bulimia.
However, due to sample size we were unable to examine whether findings differed by ED type.

It is therefore important to acknowledge that the impacts of labelling across ED types may not be not uniform (e.g., individuals with anorexia may be more negatively impacted by calories vs. individuals with binge eating disorder (19).
text.formatted: It is therefore important to acknowledge that the impacts of labelling across ED types may not be not uniform (e.g., individuals with anorexia may be more negatively impacted by calories vs. individuals with binge eating disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: In both studies, choices were hypothetical and in the absence of price considerations, which is a limitation.
However, in the real world, price would be consistent across labelling types, and hypothetical food selection task findings have been shown to directly translate into real-world behaviour (25).
text.formatted: However, in the real world, price would be consistent across labelling types, and hypothetical food selection task findings have been shown to directly translate into real-world behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, in all food selection tasks except the calorie-specific task, TLL without calories were used and calorie WL were omitted.
TLL were also applied to all products (under voluntary implementation coverage is approximately 75% of products (32)).
text.formatted: TLL were also applied to all products (under voluntary implementation coverage is approximately 75% of products <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32)</ref>).

text.text: This makes results less generalisable to the real-world as calorie information may or may not be required to be displayed in mandatory FOP labelling approaches.
However, if this was the case it may be that both WL and TLL could evoke greater negative affect among people with an ED due to displaying calorie content (19).
text.formatted: However, if this was the case it may be that both WL and TLL could evoke greater negative affect among people with an ED due to displaying calorie content <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: From a policy perspective, our findings suggest that implementation of a mandatory WL policy in the UK could reduce selection of unhealthy food.

Indeed, recent findings from Chile indicate that WL have been estimated to have reduced rates of childhood obesity in Chile since their implementation (33) and, if mandated in the UK are estimated to yield greater reductions in cardiovascular disease and obesity relative to TLL (34).
text.formatted: Indeed, recent findings from Chile indicate that WL have been estimated to have reduced rates of childhood obesity in Chile since their implementation <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(33)</ref> and, if mandated in the UK are estimated to yield greater reductions in cardiovascular disease and obesity relative to TLL <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(34)</ref>.

text.text: WL may also be more effective than TLL for individuals with lower health literacy due to their simple, clear messaging (3).

However, it would be important to engage in consultation with individuals with an ED to ascertain potential impacts of WL on ED behaviours, in addition to potential negative emotional impacts assessed here.
Implementing TLL mandatorily would be a positive (but likely less impactful on food choice) alternative step and would be received favourably by the UK public based on our findings.
Due to the voluntary nature of the current TLL policy in the UK, an estimated quarter of products (often unhealthy) do not to display the label (32).
text.formatted: Due to the voluntary nature of the current TLL policy in the UK, an estimated quarter of products (often unhealthy) do not to display the label <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32)</ref>.

text.text: Other TLL improvements indicated in related research should also be considered, including design and portion size consistency (14).
text.formatted: Other TLL improvements indicated in related research should also be considered, including design and portion size consistency <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, WL appears to be more effective than TLL in changing hypothetical food selection among individuals without an ED, and tentatively individuals with an ED.
There were no substantial negative emotional effects observed in response to either label, relative to no label, although mandatory implementation of TLL may initially be more publicly acceptable.
The UK Government should consider a mandatory FOP WL strategy or substantial improvements to the current FOP TLL strategy.

In Study 2, an ANCOVA controlling for the number of unhealthy food items selected during the baseline no-label task indicated a significant effect of follow-up label condition, F(2, 236) = 4.12, p = .017, partial η² = .034.

Participants in the WL condition selected fewer unhealthy food items at follow-up (M = 1.80, SD = 1.42) than participants in the TLL (M = 2.39, SD = 1.26) and control conditions (M = 2.40, SD = 1.10).

Planned comparisons of baseline-adjusted means indicated that participants in the WL condition selected fewer unhealthy items than participants in the control condition (adjusted mean difference = -0.46, p = .007) and TLL condition (adjusted mean difference = -0.37, p = .030).
The TLL and control condition did not significantly differ (adjusted mean difference = -0.09, p = .581).
In Study 2, there was also no significant effect of label condition on total calories selected F(2, 236) = 1.16, p = .316, partial η² = .010.

However, there was a significant effect of label condition on total fat (F(2, 235) = 8.65, p < .001, partial η² = .069), saturated fat (F(2, 224) = 17.11, p < .001, partial η² = .133), sugar (F(2, 227) = 5.86, p = .003, partial η² = .049), and salt selection (F(2, 236) = 6.81, p = .001, partial η² = .055).
